feedback: Written before this candidate has raced, so no result is stated for it. What I had to do in the controller: nothing beyond keeping the iteration 3 gains (kp 0.8, kd 0.15, ki 0), because this test changes only mass and the controller must stay fixed for the comparison. Evidence: iteration 3 (80 mm row, 0.12 m, 0.8 kg) scored 69.18, the best so far. Iteration 4 (0.10 m track, kp 0.7) scored 53.14 with s-bend progress falling from 0.156 to 0.081. Iteration 5 (0.14 m track, kp 0.93) scored 60.26, so the track optimum is near 0.12 m and that track stays fixed. Max error stays at 0.060 to 0.067 m on every track while RMS stays at 0.019 to 0.033 m, so the peak is a bend transient. Decision rules for the next race: if the score rises above 69.18 with max_error falling, keep 0.6 kg and move to the first requested change. If the score falls while steering_oscillation rises above about 0.17, the lighter robot is under-damped, so return to 0.8 kg or try mass 0.7 kg. If the score falls with oscillation unchanged, mass is not the limit, so return to 0.8 kg and test wheel_radius.
requested_changes: If 0.6 kg beats 69.18 with max_error falling, try wheel_radius 0.035 m with everything else unchanged. Iterations 3 to 5 reached only 0.12 to 0.23 of the course, so a larger wheel should give more ground speed at the same PWM (hypothesis from the progress shortfall).

If steering_oscillation rises above about 0.17 at 0.6 kg, try mass 0.7 kg alone. Iteration 1 (0.6 kg) lowered oval oscillation to 0.074 but also lowered progress, so 0.7 kg is a milder version of the same trade-off.

If line_loss_events on the slalom stay at 2.0 (iterations 0, 3, 4 and 5), try sensor_size 0.016 m on the 80 mm row as a single test. Iteration 1 changed sensor size together with other variables, so its effect is unproven.
